note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: Widespread sore, red, very itchy, and dry skin rash consistent with eczema flare.
- Onset/duration: Past few days; getting “way worse” over this period.
- Distribution: Chest, hands, arms; worst in the antecubital fossae (inside of elbows).
- Character/associated features: Very itchy; dry; cracked areas present. Denies weeping/watery discharge. No thickened/darkened skin noted. No visible scratch marks reported.
- Prior episodes: Known eczema with previous flares.
- Triggers/changes: Denies changes in usual skincare products; uses emollients daily.
- Prior treatments: Emollients (Diprobase cream; “Dermal” shower product). Over-the-counter hydrocortisone tried previously and not helpful. Previously tried an OTC antihistamine (likely cetirizine) without benefit.
- Systemic symptoms: Clinician asked about fever and joint pains, but patient did not confirm; status not documented.

Past Medical History:
- Conditions: Eczema; asthma (uses “blue inhaler” as needed; not daily).
- Allergies: No known drug allergies.
- Family history: Mother with migraine; mother also reported to have hypothyroidism (clinician restated as hyperthyroidism—conflict noted).
- Medications:
  - Diprobase emollient cream (patient-reported daily use; dose/route/frequency not fully documented).
  - “Dermal” shower product/emollient (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - OTC hydrocortisone topical previously tried; not effective (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Asthma “blue inhaler” PRN (exact medication and dosing not documented).

Physical Examination:
- Modality: Telehealth; no in-person exam.
- Reported findings: Widespread erythematous, sore, very itchy, dry rash on chest, hands, and arms; worst inside elbows. Cracked areas present. Denies weeping. No thickened/darkened skin. No scratch marks reported.
- Other systems: No confirmed reports of fever or joint pain (not documented).

Impression:
- Widespread atopic dermatitis (eczema) flare, worsening over several days.

Management Plan:
- Medications prescribed:
  - Fexofenadine (oral antihistamine); dose/frequency not documented.
  - Betnovate (topical corticosteroid): Apply small amounts (fingertip unit guidance provided) twice daily for the next couple of weeks.
- Skin care:
  - Continue emollients (Diprobase) and “Dermal” soap substitute as previously used.
- Safety/monitoring:
  - If no improvement or if worsening before 2 weeks, contact clinic.
  - Stop and seek care if any adverse reaction occurs.
- Prescription logistics:
  - Prescriptions to be sent to Boots pharmacy for collection.
- Education:
  - Fingertip unit explained; small amounts can cover large areas; avoid overuse.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with known eczema presents with a several-day history of a markedly worsened, widespread itchy and dry rash, worst in the elbow creases. No weeping; cracked areas present. Plan is to escalate topical steroid to Betnovate, add fexofenadine, and continue emollients, with close follow-up if not improving.

Key Takeaways:
- Use Betnovate twice daily in thin layers for about two weeks, following fingertip-unit guidance.
- Continue regular emollients and soap substitute.
- Call sooner if symptoms worsen or if any adverse reaction occurs; otherwise reassess if not improved in two weeks.

Next Steps:
- Begin prescribed fexofenadine and Betnovate as directed; collect from Boots.
- Monitor response over the next 1–2 weeks; contact clinic earlier if deterioration.
- Consider further evaluation or treatment escalation (e.g., different potency steroid, wet wraps, dermatology review) if inadequate response—pending follow-up.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vital signs; no in-person skin exam; no documentation of fever/joint pains confirmation; no doses/frequencies for fexofenadine; exact strength of Betnovate not specified; quantity/dispense not documented; no review of infection signs beyond weeping; no social/occupational or trigger assessment; no full medication reconciliation (asthma inhaler details absent).
- Internal conflicts: Family history recorded as hypothyroidism by patient; clinician restated as hyperthyroidism (conflict noted). Product name ambiguity: clinician said “diprovate” when advising to continue emollients; patient’s product is “Diprobase” (uncertainty noted). 
- Transcript quality: Minor interruptions and unclear brand/product names; otherwise understandable.
